Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a short announcement for a new feature in a note-taking app: offline sync. Around 200 words.

Your notes stay in sync across all your devices, whether you have an internet connection or not. Open your note-taking app on your phone, laptop, or tablet.

Make changes, add new notes, delete things — it all works offline. When you reconnect to the internet, your changes sync automatically. You'll want this if you travel without reliable wifi, work in places without coverage, or just want to write without interruptions. The app handles it. Conflicts rarely happen, but when they do, we show you both versions side by side. If you edited the same note offline on your phone and your computer, you can see both changes and decide which to keep.

Syncing is efficient — we only send what changed, not your entire note library. If your connection drops mid-sync, we resume automatically the next time you connect — nothing breaks.

Offline sync is on by default. No setup or configuration needed.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a paragraph about what happens when two devices edit the same note offline.

output:
Your notes stay in sync across all your devices, whether or not you have an internet connection. Edit from your phone, laptop, or tablet. Make changes, add notes, delete things — it all works offline.

When you reconnect to the internet, your changes sync automatically to all your devices. The sync is efficient: we only send what changed, not your entire note library. If your connection drops mid-sync, we resume automatically the next time you come back online — nothing breaks.

When the same note is edited offline on multiple devices, both versions are automatically preserved. When you reconnect, you see both sets of changes side by side. You can choose which version to keep, or manually combine the edits if they don't conflict. This situation rarely happens in practice — most people work on different notes across their various devices — but if it does happen, you have complete visibility into exactly what was changed and where.

Offline sync is turned on by default for all your devices. No setup or configuration needed.
